text.p: Concern over President Boris Yeltsin's health deepened on Wednesday despite a statement by his top aide that he was still in charge in Russia.
Kremlin chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais told the newspaper Izvestia that Yeltsin was still taking major decisions during preparations for a heart bypass operation.
"As for the key questions, despite his illness the president is not only in touch but is taking decisions," Chubais said.
But the interview, published on Wednesday, was conducted with the newspaper on Friday evening, before doctors decided to extend the president's hospital stay.
Presidential press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky said on Tuesday that Yeltsin was likely to stay in Moscow's Central Clinical Hospital until the end of this week.
Ekho Moskvy radio station voiced its concern, saying the Kremlin had indicated when Yeltsin, 65, went to hospital for tests last Friday that he would stay only for the weekend.
"There is no good news about the president's health," Ekho Moskvy said in a commentary.
Yeltsin looked relaxed in brief television pictures of him meeting Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin on Tuesday.
Chubais said Chernomyrdin and other officials were already taking some decisions which were previously taken by Yeltsin.

Ekho Moskvy dismissed a suggestion by Yastrzhembsky that Yeltsin had demonstrated his fitness by meeting Chernomyrdin for about an hour. It said Russia's problems were too big for the two men to cover them properly in just an hour.
Speculation is growing that Yeltsin's extended stay in hospital was prompted by concern that his overall state of health is not good enough for him to have major heart surgery.
"It seems the doctors do not want to operate on him because of his general physical condition," a source in the opposition Communist Party told Reuters.

Chubais raised doubts about whether Yeltsin would have the operation by saying more than a week ago that the Kremlin leader was likely to hand over his powers only briefly "if the operation which the president spoke about actually takes place".
Yeltsin has said he would be able to work only in a passive way if he did not have surgery. This could put the nature of the presidency in question and have huge political implications.
The Kremlin has denied there are any complications in Yeltsin's condition, despite persistent rumours that his liver has been damaged by drink or that he has other health problems.
But the Kremlin's newly declared policy of openness has left unanswered many questions about Yeltsin's condition and the operation he is due to have.
Doctors are due to meet on September 25 or 26 to decide when to operate to improve the blood flow to Yeltsin's heart.
Yeltsin, who had two heart attacks last year, has not said whether he will give up his duties -- including control of Russia's nuclear missiles -- for the duration of the operation.
Chubais told Izvestia the president was likely to hand his duties to Chernomyrdin for a period of 10 hours to two days.
Playing down reports of a power struggle between Chernomyrdin, security chief Alexander Lebed and himself, as well as splits over Chechnya policy, Chubais said all three men were working together.

Asked about what would happen if the conflict in Chechnya "exploded", he said: "I can tell you this: today all of us -- Lebed, Chernomyrdin and Chubais -- are obliged to do all we can to prevent the explosion you are talking about."
